title: AtomMOF: All-Atom Flow Matching for MOF-Adsorbate Structure Prediction
claim: The task maps a set of discrete building blocks and an adsorbate to a single complete all-atom periodic structure.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, large arrow between inputs and output
description: The figure defines the task as a mapping from inputs to an output. On the left, a gray rounded container titled "Building Blocks B" holds three white cards. The largest card is "Linkers x2" and shows a ball-and-stick 2D molecular diagram of a tri-aryl linker with gray carbon atoms, small white hydrogens and red oxygens. Below it are "Metals x2", a large teal circle, and "Adsorbate", a two-atom red dumbbell. A big gray arrow points right to "MOF–Adsorbate Structure S = (A, X, ℓ)". That panel shows a 3D render of the periodic framework with teal metal nodes, gray linkers and red oxygens. The unit cell is outlined in black and highlighted at full opacity, and the surrounding periodic images are faded.
caption: MOF-adsorbate structure prediction. Given building blocks B, including linkers, metal nodes, and adsorbate, the goal is to predict the equilibrium structure S = (A, X, ℓ) with atomic numbers A, coordinates X, and lattice ℓ.
abstract: Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) are promising materials for applications such as direct air capture, where performance depends on how adsorbates bind within the framework. Accurately predicting MOF-adsorbate configurations is therefore important for screening candidate materials. However, traditional approaches are computationally expensive and require a known host structure, while existing generative models rely on rigid-body assumptions and do not explicitly model adsorbates. We introduce AtomMOF, a scalable all-atom flow-matching model that jointly predicts MOF-adsorbate structures from discrete building blocks and adsorbates. Built on a Diffusion Transformer with a building block-based pairwise attention bias, AtomMOF operates in an unconstrained all-atom space and exhibits clear scaling behavior. To improve the structural validity of flexible all-atom models, we also propose Feynman-Kac (FK) steering with machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs). On the BW dataset, AtomMOF achieves a 85.61% relative increase in match rate and a 34.32% relative reduction in RMSD compared with prior work. MLIP-guided steering further improves validity by 28.7% and reduces formation energy error by 86.5%. On ODAC25, AtomMOF generates adsorption configurations faster than GCMC and, when combined with MLIP relaxation, identifies lower-energy configurations than those in the reference dataset.
